C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C005.object: unemployment among low-skilled workers only in counties with high employer concentration
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage unemployment among low-skilled workers only in counties with high employer concentration]

[PATH:empirical] Quarterly Workforce Indicators (QWI) merged with Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) data at the county-industry level — Allows direct testing of the interaction between minimum wage increases and employer concentration on county-level unemployment for low-skilled workers, using a difference-in-differences or event-study design.

[PATH:empirical] Survey of Employer Monopsony Power and Wage-Setting Behavior (e.g., from the Federal Reserve or Bureau of Labor Statistics special supplements) — Provides micro-level data on employer concentration and wage-setting practices, enabling analysis of whether high-concentration counties exhibit different employment responses to minimum wage changes.

[PATH:theoretical] Manning (2003) 'Monopsony in Motion' and subsequent theoretical models of labor market concentration — Offers a theoretical framework predicting that minimum wage increases can reduce employment only when employers have significant monopsony power, directly relevant to the hypothesis's scope and qualifiers.

scope.domain: low-skilled labor markets with monopsony power

qualifier.geographic: United States, particularly rural counties with fewer than 5 employers per industry

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage unemployment among low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Cengiz, D., Dube, A., Lindner, A., & Zipperer, B. (2019). The Effect of Minimum Wages on Low-Wage Jobs: Evidence from the United States Using a Bunching Estimator. Quarterly Journal of Economics. — This study uses a bunching estimator to analyze the impact of minimum wage increases on low-wage employment across U.S. states, providing direct empirical evidence on unemployment effects among low-skilled workers during periods of moderate inflation.

[PATH:literature] Neumark, D., & Shirley, P. (2021). Myth or Measurement: What Does the New Minimum Wage Research Say About Minimum Wages and Job Loss in the United States? NBER Working Paper 28388. — This comprehensive review synthesizes recent empirical studies on minimum wage and employment, offering a balanced assessment of the disputed hypothesis and highlighting conditions (e.g., inflation regimes) under which effects vary.

[PATH:theoretical] A theoretical model incorporating monopsonistic competition and inflation expectations, e.g., based on Manning, A. (2003). Monopsony in Motion. — Developing or applying a dynamic model of low-skilled labor markets with moderate inflation can clarify the mechanisms through which minimum wage changes affect unemployment, accounting for nominal rigidities and firm pricing power.

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage in the service industry
C007.object: employee turnover and training costs only when accompanied by increased automation investment
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in the service industry employee turnover and training costs only when accompanied by increased automation investment]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on turnover rates in U.S. urban service industries (e.g., fast food, retail) from 2020-2025, combined with state-level minimum wage increases and firm-level automation investment data (e.g., from tax filings or industry surveys). — A difference-in-differences or event-study analysis comparing turnover and training costs across firms with varying levels of automation investment before and after minimum wage hikes can directly test whether the hypothesized interaction effect holds.

[PATH:empirical] Case studies or industry reports from major quick-service restaurant chains (e.g., McDonald's, Panera) that have publicly disclosed automation adoption (e.g., self-order kiosks, automated fryers) alongside wage policy changes, supplemented by interviews or financial filings. — Firm-level qualitative and quantitative evidence can reveal whether automation investment actually moderates the relationship between minimum wage increases and turnover/training costs, providing granular insight into causal mechanisms.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical or simulation models of labor demand and turnover under minimum wage increases, incorporating firm-level automation decisions (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo's framework on automation and labor markets). — A formal model can clarify the conditions under which automation complementarity reduces turnover—e.g., by substituting for low-skill tasks or increasing job complexity—and generate testable predictions for the 2020-2025 urban U.S. context.

C008.subject: Raising the minimum wage
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage employee turnover and training costs]

[PATH:empirical] Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Quarterly Turnover Rates for Service Industry Sectors, compared with state-level minimum wage changes — Provides direct quantitative data on employee turnover before and after minimum wage increases, allowing causal inference via difference-in-differences analysis within the geographic and temporal scope.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or field experiment with service industry employers tracking training costs and retention rates post-wage hike — Captures firm-level training expenditure data and turnover metrics, addressing the specific object (training costs) and subject (employers) with high internal validity.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies focusing on labor turnover and training (e.g., from journals like Industrial Relations or Journal of Labor Economics) — Synthesizes existing empirical findings across multiple U.S. service industry contexts, helping to resolve the disputed status by identifying effect size heterogeneity and moderators.

qualifier.temporal: during the first year after implementation

C011.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C011.object: a small net positive effect on employment in high-productivity service sectors, offset by a small net negative effect in low-productivity retail sectors
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage a small net positive effect on employment in high-productivity service sectors, offset by a small net negative effect in low-productivity retail sectors]

[PATH:empirical] Sector-level panel data from national statistical agencies (e.g., BLS QCEW) on employment and wages in high-productivity service sectors (e.g., finance, tech) and low-productivity retail sectors, combined with state-level minimum wage changes over 2-year windows — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing employment changes in the two sector types following minimum wage increases, controlling for other economic factors.

[PATH:literature] Difference-in-differences meta-analysis of recent minimum wage studies that report sector-specific employment effects (e.g., Cengiz et al. 2019, Dube 2019) — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence to assess whether the hypothesized differential sector effects (positive in high-productivity, negative in low-productivity) are consistently observed across multiple studies.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of firm-level labor demand under heterogeneous productivity and wage floors (e.g., search-and-matching or monopsony model with sectoral productivity differences) — Provides causal mechanism: high-productivity firms may expand employment due to increased demand or reduced turnover, while low-productivity firms contract due to cost pressures; model predictions can be calibrated to match sector-level data.

scope.domain: national economy over 2-year horizon, sector-level analysis
